theme: Before Festus and Agrippa, “I stand on trial for hope”
readingInstruction: Read Acts 25:1-26:32. Paul appeals to Caesar, and then makes his defense before King Agrippa. His third account of his conversion ends with an appeal. Read 26:12-29 slowly.
settingTheScene: Felix is succeeded by Festus, who immediately faces the Jewish leaders’ demand to bring Paul to Jerusalem, where they plan an ambush. Paul, as a Roman citizen, exercises his right to appeal to Caesar. Before sending him to Rome, Festus consults King Agrippa II, who is familiar with Jewish customs. The hearing is an opportunity for Paul to give a full account of the gospel before the political and military leaders of the region.
observation: “And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers” (26:6).
“Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead?” (26:8).

“To open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me” (26:18).
“Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the vision from heaven” (26:19).
“To this day I have had the help that comes from God, and so I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass” (26:22).
“In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?” (26:28).
“Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am, except for these chains” (26:29).
interpretation:
Festus tells the Jews that Roman custom does not condemn a man before he has met his accusers face to face. At Caesarea, they bring many serious charges that they cannot prove. Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, asks Paul whether he is willing to go to Jerusalem for trial. Paul knows what would happen. “I appeal to Caesar.” This appeal, within a Roman citizen’s rights, takes the case to Rome and fulfills the Lord’s promise in 23:11.

When King Agrippa and his sister Bernice arrive, Festus explains his dilemma: he has no clear charge to write to the emperor. Agrippa asks to hear Paul. Paul says he considers himself fortunate to defend himself before one so familiar with Jewish customs. He tells his story: his strict Pharisaic upbringing, his persecution of the saints, and his encounter on the Damascus road. He now reports the commission with its fullest wording. Jesus said he was sending Paul “to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.” This is a summary of the gospel: darkness to light, Satan’s power to God, forgiveness and an inheritance, by faith in Christ.

Paul says, “I was not disobedient to the vision from heaven.” He declared to Jews and Gentiles that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance. For this, the Jews seized him. And yet he says, “I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass: that the Christ must suffer and, by being the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.”

Festus interrupts: “Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind.” Paul replies, “I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking the sober truth.” Then he turns to Agrippa: “King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.” Agrippa says, “In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?” Paul’s reply is full of grace: “Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am, except for these chains.” Agrippa concludes that Paul could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar. But the appeal is God’s means of bringing him to Rome.
connection: Acts 9:1-19 and 22:1-21 are the other accounts of the conversion. Isaiah 42:6-7 and 49:6 speak of opening blind eyes and being a light to the Gentiles. Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22 speak of the Christ’s suffering. 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 summarizes the gospel as Paul received it. Colossians 1:12-14 echoes the language of 26:18. 2 Timothy 4:16-18 mentions the Lord standing by him at his first defense. Philippians 1:12-14 says his imprisonment advanced the gospel. Romans 13:1-7 teaches about the state.
application:
Memorize Acts 26:18 as a summary of what conversion means.

Ask yourself Paul’s question to Agrippa: do you believe the prophets?

Think of someone who is “almost persuaded.” Pray for them as Paul did.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for opening your eyes and turning you from darkness to light.
Ask him to give you a clear testimony.
Pray for someone who is hardened against him.
